title: Episode 0: Welcome to Git Going with GitHub
description: A tour of the workshop structure, the two-day arc, and what you will accomplish.
concepts: What open source means and why it matters
The two-day workshop structure: Day 1 (browser) and Day 2 (VS Code + agents)
The learning philosophy: manual skill first, then automation
What a repository, issue, pull request, and merge are (high-level preview)
The 55 accessibility agents across 3 teams and what they do on Day 2
How the chapters, appendices, and exercises fit together
The exercise pattern: Try It, You are done when, What success feels like
Encouragement for learners who are new to the command line or Git
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome to Git Going with GitHub. I'm Alex.

[JAMIE]
And I'm Jamie. If you're arriving with a workshop link, a little uncertainty, or that feeling of, wait, what am I supposed to do first, this is for you.

[ALEX]
Exactly. This opening lesson is your orientation. We're going to make the path clear from the start: what this workshop is, how the two days fit together, how your private Learning Room works, how to get into it through GitHub Classroom, what to do when tools change, how to choose the right tool for the moment, what to listen for with a screen reader, and where to go for help.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just a welcome message. It's the map.

[ALEX]
Yes. And one of the most important promises in this course is that you are not being asked to do pretend work. This workshop is built around a real contribution path in real tools: GitHub, VS Code, Git, GitHub Copilot, and accessibility-focused contribution workflows.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with the big picture. This course guide describes the GitHub Learning Room as your workshop companion. Think of it as your base camp and table of contents for the whole experience.

[JAMIE]
And there's a note learners should hear early: the materials are actively refined.

[ALEX]
Right. Content may be updated leading up to and even during the course. That's not a warning that things are broken. It's a reminder that this is a living curriculum built around living platforms.

[JAMIE]
Which leads to the other big reminder: tools and websites change.

[ALEX]
They do. GitHub.com changes. GitHub Classroom changes. VS Code changes. Copilot changes. Browser extensions change. Agent features change. Labels move, buttons get renamed, preview features appear or disappear, account policies differ, and model availability can shift.

[JAMIE]
That can feel stressful, especially if you're using a screen reader and following instructions carefully.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. So the course teaches a durable strategy, not just a frozen screenshot. If the docs and your screen differ, orient yourself by the URL, the browser tab title, the page heading, landmarks, tab names, button labels, keyboard help, and in VS Code, the Command Palette.

[JAMIE]
So instead of thinking, the page changed, I'm lost, you think, what signals tell me where I am now?

[ALEX]
Exactly. That skill matters more than memorizing one version of a page. And if you find a mismatch, report it so the curriculum can be corrected.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, so what is the workshop structure?

[ALEX]
It's a two-day workshop with one central idea: you will make real contributions to a real open source project. Not simulated. Not practice in a fake interface. Real collaboration skills in real environments.

[JAMIE]
But the live event and the written curriculum are not exactly the same size, right?

[ALEX]
Correct. The live agenda is intentionally smaller than the full self-paced curriculum. In the live sessions, facilitators prioritize the minimum core path needed for you to make and understand a real contribution. Then the rest remains available for preparation, catch-up, remote participation, and continued work after the event.

[JAMIE]
So there's a live core, and then there's asynchronous follow-up.

[ALEX]
Yes. If something isn't covered live, that doesn't mean it's optional in the sense of unimportant. It means the full chapter set, challenge flow, solutions, podcast episodes, and Slack support are there so you can keep going. Remote participants also use the same checkpoints and evidence prompts, with written instructions available before each live block.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Walk us through the two days.

[ALEX]
Day 1 stays in the browser. You learn GitHub's web interface using only your keyboard and screen reader. The live Day 1 core path gets you through repository navigation, issues, branches, commits, and a first pull request.

[JAMIE]
And then there's more beyond the minimum live path.

[ALEX]
Right. Review practice, merge conflicts, labels, notifications, and open source culture can be stretch goals during the live event or completed later asynchronously.

[JAMIE]
Then Day 2 moves to the desktop.

[ALEX]
Yes. Day 2 is Visual Studio Code plus accessibility agents. You move from the browser into VS Code, learn GitHub Copilot, and work with the Accessibility Agents ecosystem. The live core prepares you to make a real contribution, and the async continuation gives you time to improve and submit that contribution well.

[JAMIE]
I like that there's a progression here, not a leap.

[ALEX]
That progression is very intentional. First you learn the skill manually in the browser. Navigate a repository. Work with an issue. Open a pull request. Review. Merge.

[JAMIE]
Then there's a bridge.

[ALEX]
Exactly. On many GitHub repositories, you can press the period key to open github.dev, which is VS Code in your browser. It uses familiar keyboard patterns and a VS Code-style editor without installation.

[JAMIE]
But it has limits.

[ALEX]
It does. No local terminal, no debugger in the full desktop sense, only web-compatible extensions, and not the complete desktop agent workflow.

[JAMIE]
So github.dev is a bridge, not the finish line.

[ALEX]
Well said. Once you understand the workflow in the browser, the desktop version makes more sense. Then on Day 2 you deepen the work: VS Code basics, Copilot inline suggestions, Copilot Chat, and agent-supported workflows like daily briefings, issue tracking, pull request review, analytics, and preparing an upstream contribution.

[JAMIE]
And there's a principle underneath all that.

[ALEX]
Yes. Learn the manual skill first. Then learn what automation is doing for you. Agents are helpful only if you understand the workflow they're accelerating.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before learners even begin Day 1, what should already be done?

[ALEX]
Two things matter here. First, if you want the most guided path, start with the Get Going with GitHub guide. That's the step-by-step onboarding path from getting the assignment link to knowing where to click, what challenge to open, and how to ask for help.

[JAMIE]
And second?

[ALEX]
Complete the pre-workshop setup chapter before Day 1. That includes creating a GitHub account, installing Git, setting up VS Code "” optional for Day 1, required for Day 2 "” configuring your screen reader for GitHub, and verifying that everything works.

[JAMIE]
How long should that setup take?

[ALEX]
About thirty minutes, though support is available if it takes longer. And if you can't finish every setup step before the workshop, tell a facilitator early. Setup problems are normal.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also an audio layer to the course itself, which is fitting, since we are currently in it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Every chapter and appendix has a companion podcast episode. You can listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after reading to reinforce them. There's a browseable podcast page with HTML5 players, and there's an RSS feed if you prefer a podcast app.

[JAMIE]
And the episodes are short enough to fit into real life.

[ALEX]
Yes, usually about eight to eighteen minutes. Good for a walk, a commute, or just a break from intensive screen reader navigation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's make the curriculum concrete. What does Day 1 cover?

[ALEX]
Day 1 begins with the getting-started path and pre-workshop setup, then moves into choosing your tools, understanding GitHub's web structure, navigating repositories, understanding the Learning Room, working with issues, working with pull requests, handling merge conflicts, open source culture, labels and milestones and projects, and finally notifications and a Day 1 close.

[JAMIE]
So by the end of Day 1, a learner should be able to use GitHub's web interface independently.

[ALEX]
Yes. The Day 1 self-paced total is about eight hours, but the live agenda focuses on the core path and may leave some chapters as async follow-up.

[JAMIE]
And Day 2?

[ALEX]
Day 2 covers the VS Code interface and setup, accessibility features in VS Code, the mental model of Git, Git in practice, code review with pull requests and diffs, GitHub Copilot, issue templates, fork-based contribution, accessibility agents, a capstone project, and next steps.

[JAMIE]
Which is a lot.

[ALEX]
It is. About ten hours self-paced. Live Day 2 focuses on VS Code, Git, Copilot, agent discovery, and supported contribution work, with the deeper capstone often continuing afterward.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I also don't want to skip the reference materials, because those are a real accessibility support feature, not an afterthought.

[ALEX]
I agree. The appendices are there to stay open while you work. They are not part of the linear chapter sequence. They're meant to be used at the moment you need them.

[JAMIE]
What are the big ones learners should keep handy?

[ALEX]
Always-open resources include the glossary and the screen reader cheat sheet. Beyond that, the guide also points you to the FAQ, troubleshooting guide, quick reference, glossary, screen reader cheat sheet, and a broader resources collection.

[JAMIE]
So if you hit jargon, use the glossary. If you forget a command, use quick reference. If something breaks, use troubleshooting.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And if you are still stuck, open a support issue at the Community Access support repository. Describe what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and include your screen reader and operating system.

[JAMIE]
That detail matters because support is much easier when the context is clear.

[ALEX]
Yes. "It doesn't work" is hard to diagnose. "I'm using NVDA on Windows, I activated this control, I expected a repository page, and instead I heard this" is actionable.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we leave the course guide, can we do a compact workshop-at-a-glance recap?

[ALEX]
Sure. Day 1 focuses on the GitHub web interface using a browser and screen reader. The core skills are navigate, issue, pull request, review, and merge. The outcome is that you can use GitHub independently.

[JAMIE]
And Day 2 focuses on VS Code plus accessibility agents.

[ALEX]
Right. The tools include VS Code, Copilot, and the accessibility agent ecosystem. The core skills are Git, Copilot, agents, fork-based contribution, and the capstone path. The outcome is that you have a real contribution workflow and review process you can keep using.

[JAMIE]
And if someone wants the official source of truth?

[ALEX]
Use GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. The course also includes section-level source maps so learners can verify facts by topic.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
All right. Let's shift into the guided onboarding path: getting going with GitHub.

[ALEX]
This guide starts with a reassuring premise: if you are new, unsure, or joining from a workshop link, you do not need prior knowledge of Git, GitHub, VS Code, or the command line to begin.

[JAMIE]
That's important to say out loud, because many learners assume everyone else already knows the basics.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The course is designed so you are not left guessing what comes next.

[JAMIE]
What specifically will learners have?

[ALEX]
You'll have a GitHub Classroom assignment link from the facilitator, your own private Learning Room repository, challenge issues with explicit instructions, evidence prompts telling you what to post when you finish, Gandalf bot feedback on pull requests, reference solutions you can compare against after you try, and multiple tool paths so you can work in the browser, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the command line when appropriate.

[JAMIE]
So the goal isn't speed.

[ALEX]
No. The goal is confidence through small, checkable steps.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's return to something you mentioned earlier, because it appears here too: what should learners do when tools or pages change?

[ALEX]
First, do not assume that a difference means you failed. Instead, use an exploration pattern. Check the URL and browser tab title. Move by headings, landmarks, tabs, and button names instead of relying on visual order. Open keyboard shortcut help "” on GitHub that's question mark "” or use the VS Code Command Palette if shortcuts differ. Read nearby labels before activating a control. And if needed, ask a facilitator or file a curriculum issue including the page link, the step that differed, and what you heard or observed.

[JAMIE]
So the durable skill is orient, verify, continue.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now we get to the actual starting sequence. Step one: know your starting place.

[ALEX]
Yes. Before Day 1, complete the pre-workshop setup chapter. That chapter helps you create or verify your GitHub account, configure accessibility settings, choose a browser, install Git and VS Code, and confirm your screen reader setup.

[JAMIE]
And if setup is incomplete?

[ALEX]
Tell a facilitator early. Recovery time and support are built into the workshop.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Step two is accepting the GitHub Classroom assignment. Can you walk us through that in plain language?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. At the start of Day 1, the facilitator gives you a GitHub Classroom assignment link. It usually begins with classroom dot github dot com slash a slash.

[JAMIE]
And you should open it in the browser where you're already signed in to GitHub.

[ALEX]
Correct. Then, if GitHub asks you to authorize GitHub Classroom, activate the authorize button. If you're asked to choose your name from a roster, select your name. If your name is missing, use the skip option and tell the facilitator. Then activate Accept this assignment.

[JAMIE]
And then wait.

[ALEX]
Yes. GitHub Classroom needs a moment to create your private repository. Refresh until the repository link appears, open it, and bookmark it.

[JAMIE]
And the repository name usually follows a pattern.

[ALEX]
Something like learning-room-your-username. That repository is your personal practice space.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Which takes us to step three: understanding the Learning Room itself.

[ALEX]
The Learning Room is a private repository created from a template. Everyone begins with the same materials, but your work belongs to you.

[JAMIE]
Why is that such a useful design?

[ALEX]
Because it gives you a safe place to practice real GitHub workflows. You have your own issues, branches, commits, and pull requests. Other students do not see your work unless pairing is intentional. Mistakes are expected and recoverable. Bot feedback is educational, not punitive. And challenge issues unlock in sequence, so you always know the next step.

[JAMIE]
I love the phrase guided practice studio.

[ALEX]
That's exactly what it is. Real GitHub, but with scaffolding.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Step four is finding Challenge 1.

[ALEX]
Once the Learning Room is created, the Student Progression Bot opens your first challenge issue.

[JAMIE]
So what does the learner do?

[ALEX]
Open your Learning Room repository. Go to the Issues tab "” on GitHub the shortcut is G then I. Find the issue titled Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around. Open it and read the issue body from top to bottom. Follow the checklist. Post your evidence in the requested place, either in the evidence field or as a comment. Then close the challenge issue when the instructions tell you to close it.

[JAMIE]
And closing one challenge triggers the next.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You do not have to hunt through the whole course wondering what comes next. The sequence is designed to reveal the next step when you finish the current one.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Step five is tool choice, and I think this is where learners sometimes get anxious. They worry there's one right tool.

[ALEX]
There isn't. The workshop teaches the workflow first, then gives you multiple tool paths.

[JAMIE]
Can we do the plain-language version?

[ALEX]
Yes. GitHub.com in the browser is best for Day 1, issues, pull requests, repository navigation, and reviews. github.dev is best when you want a VS Code-style editor in the browser without installing anything; on many repository pages, press period to open it. VS Code desktop is best for Day 2, local Git, Copilot, extensions, and deeper editing. GitHub Desktop is best if you want a desktop Git workflow without typing Git commands. GitHub CLI is best if you prefer terminal workflows or want automation later.

[JAMIE]
And whichever tool you use, the important thing is understanding the contribution workflow.

[ALEX]
Yes: issue, branch, change, commit, pull request, review, merge. Tools may differ, but that conceptual path stays consistent.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Step six is especially for screen reader users: what to listen for.

[ALEX]
When you feel lost, listen for structure before taking action. Useful signals include the page title, the repository name heading, landmark names like main content or repository navigation, tab names like Code, Issues, and Pull requests, the issue title, the pull request title, the branch name, button names, field labels, and bot comments or check results.

[JAMIE]
So if I'm unsure where I am, I shouldn't panic. I should pause and navigate by headings or landmarks.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Re-orienting is part of the workflow. It is not evidence that you're doing something wrong.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Step seven is using the support built into the course.

[ALEX]
And there's quite a lot of it. Every challenge issue includes instructions and evidence prompts. Every chapter has an If You Get Stuck section. Every challenge has a reference solution in the solutions folder. Gandalf bot posts feedback on pull requests. The Student Progression Bot opens the next challenge when you finish the current one. Facilitators and peers are part of the support system too.

[JAMIE]
So the advice is: don't silently restart from scratch.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Read the latest bot message, check the challenge issue, and ask for help with the link to the page where you got stuck.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then step eight is a first success check.

[ALEX]
Yes. You are ready to continue when you can say four things: I can open my Learning Room repository. I can find the Issues tab. I can open Challenge 1. And I know where to post my evidence and how to ask for help.

[JAMIE]
That's such a healthy checkpoint, because it doesn't require mastery of everything.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You do not need to understand every GitHub feature before beginning. You just need enough orientation to take the next step.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So where should learners go next if they want the gentlest path?

[ALEX]
Use this order: pre-workshop setup, choose your tools, understand GitHub, navigate repositories, understand the Learning Room, and then complete your Challenge 1 issue in your own repository.

[JAMIE]
And I think the final line of that guide is worth repeating in spirit.

[ALEX]
Yes. You belong here. The path is meant to stay explicit, and the course keeps giving you the next step.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap, let's make sure we include the administrative details learners may need later.

[ALEX]
Good idea. For current factual reference, use GitHub Docs and the GitHub Changelog. The course materials also include section-level source maps showing which official sources back which sections.

[JAMIE]
And if a learner needs immediate practical backup during the workshop?

[ALEX]
Keep the reference materials nearby: glossary, screen reader cheat sheet, troubleshooting, quick reference, FAQ, and the resources collection. If you're still stuck, open a support issue with clear details about what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and which screen reader and operating system you're using.

[JAMIE]
So the through line of this whole episode is: this workshop is real, but it is also structured.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Real tools, real workflows, real contributions, but also clear guidance, private practice space, progressive challenges, bot feedback, accessible orientation strategies, and multiple ways to continue when something changes.

[JAMIE]
That feels like a good place to land. You do not have to know everything. You do need a starting place.

[ALEX]
And now you have one. Open your setup chapter if you haven't completed it yet. Accept your GitHub Classroom assignment when your facilitator provides it. Bookmark your Learning Room. Find Challenge 1. And keep moving one checkable step at a time.

[JAMIE]
We'll meet you in the next part.

headings.title: GitHub Learning Room - Your Complete Workshop Companion

sourceFiles.content:
# Course Guide
>
> **Listen to Episode 0:** [Welcome to Git Going with GitHub](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

## GitHub Learning Room - Your Complete Workshop Companion

> **Welcome.** You are about to begin a two-day journey into open source collaboration using GitHub, VS Code, and GitHub Copilot - all designed for screen reader and keyboard-only navigation. This guide is your starting point and table of contents for everything in this workshop.
>
> **Note:** Workshop content is being actively refined for the May 2026 cohort. Students should expect updates to materials leading up to and during the course.

> **Important: tools and websites change.** GitHub.com, GitHub Classroom, VS Code, GitHub Copilot, github.dev, browser extensions, and agent experiences are living products. We do our best to keep this curriculum current and source-backed, but labels, page order, shortcuts, preview features, model availability, and account-policy behavior can shift. If the documentation and your screen differ, use the exploration pattern taught in Chapters 2 and 3: orient by URL, page title, H1, landmarks, tab names, button labels, keyboard help, and the VS Code Command Palette. Then report the mismatch so the documentation can be corrected.

## How This Course Works

This is a two-day workshop built around one idea: **you will make real contributions to a real open source project.** Not simulated. Not pretend. Real.

### Live Agenda and Self-Paced Curriculum

The live hackathon agenda is intentionally smaller than the full curriculum. Live sessions prioritize the core contribution path, while the complete chapter set remains available for self-paced preparation, catch-up, remote participation, and post-event continuation.

- **Live core:** The facilitator chooses the minimum path needed for participants to make and understand a real contribution.
- **Async follow-up:** Chapters and challenges not covered live can be completed after the session using the Learning Room, solutions, podcasts, and Slack channel.
- **Remote participation:** Remote cohorts should use the same checkpoints and evidence prompts, with written instructions available before each live block.

### The Two Days

#### Day 1 - GitHub Foundations (Browser)

You learn GitHub's web interface using only your keyboard and screen reader. The live Day 1 core path gets you through repository navigation, issues, branches, commits, and a first pull request. Review practice, merge conflicts, labels, notifications, and culture exercises remain available as stretch or async follow-up.

#### Day 2 - VS Code + Accessibility Agents (Desktop)

You move to Visual Studio Code, learn GitHub Copilot, and activate the Accessibility Agents ecosystem. The live Day 2 core path prepares you to make a real contribution, and the async continuation path gives you time to polish and submit it well.

### The Journey Arc

```text
Day 1 - Learn the skill in the browser
  Navigate → Issue → Pull Request → Review → Merge

     ↓  (bridge: press . on any GitHub repo - VS Code opens in your browser)

github.dev - VS Code on the web, no install needed
  Same keyboard shortcuts · Same screen reader mode · Edit files · Open PRs
  Limits: no local terminal or debugger, only web-compatible extensions, and not the full desktop agent workflow

     ↓  (you've earned the desktop - now it makes sense)

Day 2 - Deepen with VS Code + Accessibility Agents
  VS Code basics → Copilot inline → Copilot Chat
  @daily-briefing → @issue-tracker → @pr-review → @analytics → prepare upstream
```

**The key principle:** Learn the manual skill first, then see how it is automated. The agents only make sense when you already understand what they are doing.

## Before You Begin

Start with **[Get Going with GitHub](get-going.md)** if you want the most guided path. It explains how GitHub Classroom creates your private Learning Room repository, how Challenge 1 appears, how evidence prompts work, and how to choose between browser, github.dev, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, and command-line paths.

Complete everything in **[Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup](00-pre-workshop-setup.md)** before Day 1. This chapter walks you through:

- Creating a GitHub account
- Installing Git
- Setting up VS Code (optional for Day 1, required for Day 2)
- Configuring your screen reader for GitHub
- Verifying everything works

**Time needed:** About 30 minutes.

## Companion Audio Series

Every chapter and appendix has a companion podcast episode - a conversational two-host overview that previews or reviews the key concepts. Listen before reading a chapter to know what to expect, or after to reinforce what you learned.

- **[Browse the podcast episodes](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html)** with HTML5 audio players
- **[Subscribe via RSS](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/feed.xml)** in your preferred podcast app
- Episodes are 8-18 minutes each - perfect for commutes, walks, or screen reader breaks

## Day 1: GitHub Foundations

These chapters are designed to be read and practiced in order. Each builds on the one before it.

| # | Chapter | What You Will Learn | Time |
|---|---------|-------------------|------|
| [Start](get-going.md) | **Get Going with GitHub** | GitHub Classroom onboarding, Learning Room first steps, support, and tool choice | 15 min |
| [00](00-pre-workshop-setup.md) | **Pre-Workshop Setup** | Install and configure everything before Day 1 | 30 min |
| [01](01-choose-your-tools.md) | **Choose Your Adventure: A Tool Tour** | Explore the 5 tool environments before you start | 30 min |
| [02](02-understanding-github.md) | **Understanding GitHub's Web Structure** | How GitHub is organized - page types, headings, landmarks, screen reader orientation | 1 hr |
| [03](03-navigating-repositories.md) | **Navigating Repositories** | Explore any repo using your screen reader - tabs, files, commits, branches | 45 min |
| [04](04-the-learning-room.md) | **The Learning Room** | Your shared practice environment - challenges, PR workflow, bot feedback, peer review | 30 min |
| [05](05-working-with-issues.md) | **Working with Issues** | File, search, filter, comment on, and manage issues | 1 hr |
| [06](06-working-with-pull-requests.md) | **Working with Pull Requests** | Create, review, comment on, and merge pull requests | 1 hr |
| [07](07-merge-conflicts.md) | **Merge Conflicts** | Understand why conflicts happen and how to resolve them | 1 hr |
| [08](08-open-source-culture.md) | **Open Source Culture and Contributing** | Communication, tone, reviews, inclusive language, your first contribution | 30 min |
| [09](09-labels-milestones-projects.md) | **Labels, Milestones and Projects** | Organize and cross-reference work | 45 min |
| [10](10-notifications-and-day-1-close.md) | **Notifications and Day 1 Close** | Manage your inbox, @mentions, and subscriptions; recap Day 1 | 30 min |

**Day 1 self-paced total:** ~8 hours. The live Day 1 agenda covers the core path in a shorter Pacific-time event day and treats later challenges as stretch or async follow-up.

## Day 2: VS Code + Accessibility Agents

Day 2 moves you from the browser to the desktop. Every skill maps directly to what you learned on Day 1.

| # | Chapter | What You Will Learn | Time |
|---|---------|-------------------|------|
| [11](11-vscode-interface.md) | **VS Code: Interface and Setup** | Launch VS Code, sign in, screen reader mode, Activity Bar, Settings, shortcuts | 45 min |
| [12](12-vscode-accessibility.md) | **VS Code: Accessibility Deep Dive** | Keyboard navigation, Problems panel, Terminal, Copilot Chat, Accessible Help/View/Diff, Signals, Speech | 45 min |
| [13](13-how-git-works.md) | **How Git Works: The Mental Model** | Commits, branches, local vs remote, push/pull/fetch, why conflicts happen | 30 min |
| [14](14-git-in-practice.md) | **Git in Practice** | Clone, branch, stage, commit, push, merge - all from VS Code | 1 hr |
| [15](15-code-review.md) | **Code Review: PRs, Diffs, and Feedback** | PR extension, accessible diffs, inline comments, the reviewer's craft | 1.5 hrs |
| [16](16-github-copilot.md) | **GitHub Copilot** | Inline suggestions, Copilot Chat, effective prompting, custom instructions | 1 hr |
| [17](17-issue-templates.md) | **Issue Templates** | Create and customize GitHub issue templates with YAML | 1 hr |
| [18](18-fork-and-contribute.md) | **Fork and Contribute** | The complete fork-based open source contribution workflow | 45 min |
| [19](19-accessibility-agents.md) | **Accessibility Agents** | Agent files, prompts, skills, and contribution paths across the ecosystem | 1 hr |
| [20](20-build-your-agent.md) | **Capstone Project** | Choose Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another project and create an impactful agentic contribution | 1.5 hrs |
| [22](22-what-comes-next.md) | **What Comes Next** | Graduation, portfolio, continued learning, community | 30 min |

**Day 2 self-paced total:** ~10 hours. The live Day 2 agenda focuses on VS Code, Git, Copilot, agent discovery, and supported contribution work; deeper capstone material can continue asynchronously.

## Appendices - Reference Material

Open these at any time during the workshop. They are not part of the chapter sequence - use them when you need them.

### Always Open (Bookmark These)

| Appendix | Document | What It Covers |
|----------|----------|---------------|
| [A](appendix-a-glossary.md) | **Glossary** | Every term, concept, and piece of jargon explained |
| [B](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md) | **Screen Reader Cheat Sheet** | NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver navigation commands plus GitHub keyboard shortcuts |

### Core Reference (C-D)

| Appendix | Document | What It Covers |
|----------|----------|---------------|
| [C](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md) | **Markdown and GitHub Flavored Markdown** | Complete guide from basics through GFM - headings, lists, links, tables, alerts, Mermaid, math, footnotes |
| [D](appendix-d-git-authentication.md) | **Git Authentication** | SSH keys, Personal Access Tokens, credential storage, commit signing |

### Git Deep Dive (E-F)

| Appendix | Document | What It Covers |
|----------|----------|---------------|

# Get Going with GitHub

> **Start here if you are new, unsure, or joining from a workshop link.** This guide walks you from "I have the link" to "I know where I am, what to do next, and how to ask for help." You do not need to know Git, GitHub, VS Code, or the command line before you begin.

## What This Guide Does

This workshop is designed so you are never left guessing what comes next. You will have:

- A GitHub Classroom assignment link from the facilitator
- Your own private Learning Room repository
- Challenge issues that tell you exactly what to do
- Evidence prompts that tell you what to post when you finish
- Gandalf bot feedback on pull requests
- Reference solutions you can compare against after you try
- Multiple tool paths, so you can work in the browser, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or the command line when appropriate

The goal is not to rush. The goal is to build confidence one checkable step at a time.

## When Tools or Pages Change

GitHub.com, GitHub Classroom, VS Code, GitHub Copilot, github.dev, browser extensions, and agent tools change often. This course is actively maintained, and we use official sources and live checks wherever possible, but your screen may not always match the exact wording in a step.

When that happens, do not assume you are failing. Use the same exploration skills the workshop teaches:

1. Check the URL and browser tab title.
2. Move by headings, landmarks, tabs, and button names instead of relying only on visual order.
3. Open keyboard shortcut help (`?` on GitHub) or the VS Code Command Palette when a shortcut or control differs.
4. Read the surrounding labels before activating a control.
5. Ask a facilitator or file a curriculum issue with the page link, the step that differed, and what you heard or observed.

The durable skill is not memorizing one layout. The durable skill is learning how to orient, verify, and continue when a tool changes.

## Step 1 - Know Your Starting Place

Before Day 1 starts, complete [Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup](00-pre-workshop-setup.md). That chapter helps you create or verify your GitHub account, configure accessibility settings, choose a browser, install Git and VS Code, and confirm your screen reader setup.

If you cannot finish every setup step before the workshop, tell a facilitator early. Setup problems are normal, and the workshop is designed with time and support for recovery.

## Step 2 - Accept the GitHub Classroom Assignment

At the start of the workshop, the facilitator gives you a GitHub Classroom assignment link. It usually starts with `https://classroom.github.com/a/`. This single assignment covers both Day 1 and Day 2 content -- Day 2 challenges automatically unlock after you complete Day 1.

1. Open the assignment link in the browser where you are signed in to GitHub.
2. If GitHub asks you to authorize GitHub Classroom, activate **Authorize GitHub Classroom**.
3. If you are asked to choose your name from a roster, find your name and select it. If your name is missing, use the skip option and tell the facilitator.
4. Activate **Accept this assignment**.
5. Wait while GitHub Classroom creates your private repository.
6. Refresh the page until the repository link appears.
7. Open the repository link and bookmark it.

Your repository name usually looks like `learning-room-your-username`. This is your personal practice space for the workshop.

## Step 3 - Understand the Learning Room

The Learning Room is a private repository created from a template. Everyone starts from the same materials, but your work belongs to you.

You can safely practice there because:

- You have your own issues, branches, commits, and pull requests
- Other students do not see your work unless the facilitator intentionally pairs you
- Mistakes are expected and recoverable
- Bot feedback is educational, not punitive
- Challenge issues unlock in sequence so you always know the next step

Think of the Learning Room as a guided practice studio. It is real GitHub, but the room is set up so you can learn without fear of damaging a public project.

## Step 4 - Find Challenge 1

After your Learning Room repository is created, the Student Progression Bot creates your first challenge issue.

1. Open your Learning Room repository.
2. Navigate to the **Issues** tab. On GitHub, the keyboard shortcut is `G` then `I`.
3. Find an issue titled **Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around**.
4. Open the issue and read the body from top to bottom.
5. Follow the checklist in the issue.
6. Post your evidence in the evidence field or as the requested comment.
7. Close the challenge issue when the instructions tell you to close it.

When you close a challenge issue, the next challenge opens. You do not need to hunt through the whole curriculum to know what is next.

## Step 5 - Choose the Tool That Fits the Moment

There is no single correct way to use GitHub. The workshop teaches the workflow first, then offers tool paths.

Use this plain-language guide to decide where to start:

- **GitHub.com in the browser:** Best for Day 1, issues, pull requests, repository navigation, and reviews.
- **github.dev:** Best when you want a VS Code-style editor in the browser without installing anything. Press the period key from many repository pages to open it.
- **VS Code desktop:** Best for Day 2, local Git, Copilot, extensions, and deeper editing work.
- **GitHub Desktop:** Best if you want a desktop Git workflow without typing Git commands.
- **GitHub CLI:** Best if you prefer terminal workflows or want automation later.

You are not behind if you use one tool longer than someone else. The important skill is understanding the contribution workflow: issue, branch, change, commit, pull request, review, and merge.

## Step 6 - What to Listen For with a Screen Reader

When you feel lost, listen for structure before you take action.

Useful signals include:

- Page title
- Repository name heading
- Landmark names such as main content or repository navigation
- Tab names such as Code, Issues, and Pull requests
- Issue title
- Pull request title
- Branch name
- Button name
- Field label
- Bot comment or check result

If you are not sure where you are, pause and navigate by headings or landmarks. Finding your position is part of the workflow, not a failure.

## Step 7 - Use the Support Built into the Course

You have several safety nets.

- Every challenge issue includes instructions and evidence prompts.
- Every chapter has an **If You Get Stuck** section.
- Every challenge has a reference solution in [the solutions folder (external)](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/tree/main/docs/solutions/).
- Gandalf posts feedback on pull requests.
- The Student Progression Bot opens the next challenge when you finish the current one.
- Facilitators and peers are part of the learning system.

If something does not work, do not start over silently. Read the latest bot message, check the challenge issue, and ask for help with the link to the page where you are stuck.

## Step 8 - Your First Success Check

You are ready to continue when you can say these four things:

1. I can open my Learning Room repository.
2. I can find the Issues tab.
3. I can open Challenge 1.
4. I know where to post my evidence and how to ask for help.

That is enough. You do not need to understand every GitHub feature before you begin. The workshop will guide you one step at a time.

## Where to Go Next

Use this order if you want the gentlest path:

1. [Chapter 00: Pre-Workshop Setup](00-pre-workshop-setup.md)
2. [Chapter 01: Choose Your Tools](01-choose-your-tools.md)
3. [Chapter 02: Understanding GitHub](02-understanding-github.md)
4. [Chapter 03: Navigating Repositories](03-navigating-repositories.md)
5. [Chapter 04: The Learning Room](04-the-learning-room.md)
6. Your **Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around** issue in your Learning Room repository

You belong here. We will keep the path explicit, and we will keep giving you the next step.

## Authoritative Sources

Use these official references when you need the current source of truth for facts in this chapter.

- [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)
- [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

### Section-Level Source Map

Use this map to verify facts for each major section in this file.

- **What This Guide Does:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)
- **When Tools or Pages Change:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/), [GitHub Pages docs](https://docs.github.com/en/pages), [GitHub Pages quickstart](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/quickstart)
- **Where to Go Next:** [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en), [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.

[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
